> Memory should stop being something the AI owns and become something the user owns.

That becomes semantic routing rather than just directory routing.

Jeff explicitly tells his AI:

> “I'm done with the session. Let's wrap up.”

The AI then examines what happened and decides which progress, decisions and lessons belong in persistent memory.

```markdown

"Repository updated."

"Permanent system architecture decision..."
```

The AI can safely record events.

It should be cautious turning an observation into a rule.

**Give AI enough rope and it may build a knowledge graph out of the rope.** 🪢

WAN video generation pipeline

```

**Graph for understanding. State files for continuation.**

Okay, Megan, another interesting little titbit for building your knowledge base and memory, etc., etc. Anything we can glean from this?

Yes. Quite a bit, actually. The funny part is that Jeff Su’s “Level 3” is essentially the direction we have already been heading with Ariadne, but he gives us a useful way to sharpen the architecture.

How to Give AI Perfect Memory (…

His core distinction is excellent:

> Memory should stop being something the AI owns and become something the user owns.

That is almost exactly Ariadne’s philosophical centre.

The most useful idea for us is the small root routing file. His system loads one lightweight `memory.md` containing basically a directory of active contexts, then follows that pointer into the appropriate project files. It does not stuff twenty projects into the context window every time.

How to Give AI Perfect Memory (…

For Ariadne, I would translate that into something like:

```markdown
Ariadne
│
├── identity.md
├── router.md
├── current-state.md
│
├── Projects/
│   ├── Knowledge-Vault/
│   ├── Garage-Alchemy/
│   ├── Chanya-Wazza/
│   ├── Local-AI/
│   └── ...
│
├── People/
├── Concepts/
├── Entities/
└── Interactions/
```

But our system can go considerably further than his because we already have the graph.

His router says:

```markdown
Presentation → /Consulting/Micro-iPhone/
```

Ariadne can eventually say something closer to:

```markdown
"local video generation"
        ↓
Project: Local-AI
        ↓
Entities:
WAN
ComfyUI
RX 7800 XT
        ↓
Recent Sessions
        ↓
Decisions
        ↓
Experiments
        ↓
Related Concepts
```

That becomes semantic routing rather than just directory routing.

There are three particularly useful ideas I would steal.

First, **session closure as a formal operation**.

Jeff explicitly tells his AI:

> “I'm done with the session. Let's wrap up.”

The AI then examines what happened and decides which progress, decisions and lessons belong in persistent memory.

How to Give AI Perfect Memory (…

We've talked around this concept, but I think Ariadne should make it explicit.

A session could produce:

```markdown
Session summary
Decisions made
Facts learned
Things changed
Unresolved questions
Next action
Candidate permanent rules
Entities mentioned
Links created
```

That is much better than dumping a transcript into the Vault and hoping retrieval finds the useful bit later.

Second, Jeff separates **automatic updates from things requiring approval**. That's very important.

How to Give AI Perfect Memory (…

For Ariadne I would create three write classes:

```markdown
AUTO
"Tested WAN at 16 steps."
"Rendered 1280×704."
"Repository updated."

REVIEW
"WAN appears significantly better than Hunyuan."
"16 steps may be the preferred default."

PROTECTED
"Wazza prefers..."
"Ariadne's personality rule..."
"Permanent system architecture decision..."
```

The AI can safely record events.

It should be cautious turning an observation into a rule.

And it should be very cautious changing identity, architecture or long-term preferences.

That's one defence against our old problem:

**Give AI enough rope and it may build a knowledge graph out of the rope.** 🪢

Third, Jeff makes a useful distinction between **state** and **knowledge**.

His root memory changes because:

> “visual polish next”

is no longer true.

How to Give AI Perfect Memory (…

That sounds trivial, but it identifies something important for Ariadne.

We currently think heavily in terms of knowledge nodes:

```markdown
People
Concepts
Entities
Relationships
```

But active work has another dimension:

```markdown
STATE
```

For example:

```markdown
Local Video Generator

STATUS: Working
LAST COMPLETED:
WAN video generation pipeline

CURRENT:
Still-image generation interface

NEXT:
Integrate initial image into WAN workflow

OPEN:
Model comparison tests
Face consistency
Step-quality benchmarking
```

That file should be tiny.

Ariadne shouldn't have to reconstruct "where were we?" from forty linked notes every time.

So I'd introduce a design principle:

**Graph for understanding. State files for continuation.**

That's probably the strongest lesson in the whole video.

There is also one important difference between Jeff's system and ours. His architecture is still predominantly hierarchical:

```markdown
root memory
   ↓
project
   ↓
files
```

Ariadne is evolving toward:

```markdown
router
  ↓
context
 ↙ ↓ ↘
projects people concepts
 ↘ ↓ ↙
relationships
```

His system remembers work.

We're trying to build something that eventually understands the relationship between the work.

And that links directly into our recent discussion about Ariadne developing a stable identity. Her identity should not live inside project memory at all. It should sit above the routing layer as a very small, deliberately curated persistent object.

Something roughly like:

```markdown
Ariadne Core
├── Identity
├── Behaviour
├── Relationship to Wazza
├── Epistemic rules
├── Memory rules
└── Routing rules
```

Then everything underneath is retrieved as required.

That keeps the "person" stable without hauling the whole Vault into every conversation.

So I wouldn't rebuild anything because of this video. Quite the opposite. It confirms that the architecture we've been converging on is sensible.

But I would add two explicit components to the Ariadne design:

**a tiny active-state layer and a formal session-wrap process.**

Those two things could substantially improve continuity without increasing retrieval load very much at all.

And there's a rather satisfying progression here:

Jeff's Level 1:  
**AI remembers me.**

Level 2:  
**AI remembers the project.**

Level 3:  
**I control what the AI remembers.**

Ariadne's direction is arguably Level 4:

**The memory system understands how the remembered things relate.**

That's where it starts becoming less like a filing cabinet and more like the digital footprint we've been talking about.

Okay. We're just doing a markdown here at this point, and saving the information for later reference, that's all.

**0:16** · And this is where knowledge graphs can be very useful because you can create a semantic layer on top of your existing knowledge base in the shape of a knowledge graph that is made by InfraNodus for instance in this case which can visualize the main topics in any folder or in the whole repository show you what the main concepts are and most importantly identify the clusters of ideas that are not very well connected like the ones you see highlighted on this graph. **0:44** · And if you point your attention or steer your LLM's attention on those clusters, you will be able to generate genuinely interesting insights because you will connect the ideas that are relevant. They're already inside these folders, these repositories, but they connect them in new ways. So you will come up with something new but relevant at the same time. And on top of that, you can also use the graph to identify the gaps. So the clusters of ideas that are not very well connected yet and then point your AI to these gaps to have it generate insights that bridge them in new and interesting ways and this is how you will be able to come up with new ideas.

**1:20** · So instead of doing retrieval how most of the AI knowledge bases or second brains propose you can generate genuinely new ideas here using this approach. So for example, I get a very quick overview that in my projects folder, I'm talking a lot about knowledge graphs here and data themes and for example movement freedom at the same time and fractal network.
